name: Saturnalia
desc: Saturnalia was an ancient Roman festival in honour of the god Saturn, held on 17 December in the Julian calendar and extended by the 1st century BCE to 23 December, seven days in all. It opened with a sacrifice at the Temple of Saturn in the Roman Forum and a public banquet, followed by gift-giving, gambling and a licence in which masters served their slaves at table and a "King of the Saturnalia" presided over the merrymaking. In 217 BCE, after the Roman defeat at the Battle of Lake Trasimene, the festival was reformed with sacrifices in the Greek manner. It remained popular into the 3rd and 4th centuries CE and may have influenced later midwinter customs of western Europe.

name: Yule
desc: Yule is a winter festival and time of the year observed by heathen Germanic peoples and later merged with Christmas during Christianisation. Its earliest record is a Gothic calendar in the Codex Ambrosianus of c. 350 CE, and the English historian Bede, writing c. 726 CE, recorded that the heathen Anglo-Saxons called both December and January Giuli. Old Norse sources describe a festival in which feasting, ceremonial drinking and oath swearing were central. According to Hákonar saga góða, Hákon the Good passed a law in Norway that set Yule at the time when Christians celebrated Christmas. Yule and its cognates still name Christmas in English and other Northern European languages.

name: Dongzhi
desc: Dongzhi is the 22nd solar term of the Chinese calendar, marking the winter solstice, and the festival that Chinese people observe at that time, around 21 to 23 December. Its origins are traced to the philosophy of yin and yang, the lengthening days representing positive energy. The festival was first celebrated during the Zhou dynasty (1045 BCE–256 BCE) and declared an official celebration during the Han dynasty (206 BCE–220 CE), when people took a break from work, worshipped heaven and honoured their ancestors. Families still gather to eat tangyuan, balls of glutinous rice that symbolize reunion, and dumplings; in Korea, where the day is called Dongji, porridge is made with red beans.

name: Yalda Night
desc: Yalda Night, also called Chilla Night, is an ancient festival celebrated on the winter solstice of the Northern Hemisphere in Iran, Kurdistan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Afghanistan, Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan. On the longest night of the year friends and family gather to eat, drink and read poetry, especially Hafez, late into the night; pomegranates and watermelons are particularly significant. In Zoroastrian tradition the night was inauspicious, and its customs were originally intended to protect people from evil. The name Yalda was borrowed from Syriac-speaking Christians, in whose language it means "birth". It was added to UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage Lists in December 2022.

name: Christmas
desc: Christmas is a religious and cultural celebration commemorating the birth of Jesus Christ, observed primarily on 25 December; part of the Eastern Christian churches keep it on 25 December of the Julian calendar, which currently corresponds to 7 January. The Gospels of Luke and Matthew describe Jesus as born in Bethlehem to the Virgin Mary. The earliest document to place the birth on 25 December is the Chronograph of 354, in a part generally agreed to have been written in Rome in 336; the day was the traditional date of the winter solstice in the Roman Empire. Puritans prohibited the celebration in England from 1647 to 1660. Its customs mix pre-Christian, Christian and secular themes.

name: Advent
desc: Advent is a season observed in most Christian denominations as a time of waiting and preparation for the celebration of Jesus's birth at Christmas and for his return at the Second Coming. In Western Christianity it begins on the fourth Sunday before Christmas and opens the liturgical year; its name comes from the Latin adventus, "coming". When the season began is not known, though it existed from about 480, and the Council of Tours of 567 ordered monks to fast every day in December until Christmas. A fast kept from St. Martin's Day on 11 November, known as St Martin's Lent, was limited to the diocese of Tours until the sixth century. Practices today include Advent calendars and wreaths.

name: Epiphany
desc: Epiphany, known as Theophany in Eastern Christian tradition, is a Christian feast day commemorating the visit of the Magi, the baptism of Jesus and the wedding at Cana, traditionally on 6 January. It may have originated in the Greek-speaking east of the Roman Empire as a feast of the baptism of Jesus; the earliest reference to it as a Christian feast, by Ammianus Marcellinus, dates from 361. Western Christianity principally commemorates the Magi's visit to the Christ Child, seen as his manifestation to the Gentiles, while Eastern Christians commemorate his baptism in the River Jordan. Eastern Churches that follow the Julian calendar observe the feast on 19 January of the Gregorian calendar.

name: Koliada
desc: Koliada, or koleda, is the traditional Slavic name for the period from Christmas to Epiphany or, more generally, for Christmas-related rituals, some of which date to pre-Christian times. It denotes a festival held at the end of December to honour the sun at the winter solstice, and one theory derives it from the ancient calendae. The word originated in Old Church Slavonic, and in several Slavic languages its meaning has shifted to the custom of going from house to house on Christmas Eve, when groups of singers called koledari sing carols and receive gifts in return. The Dubrovnik kolenda, first mentioned in the 13th century, is one of the oldest recorded traditions of this kind in Croatia.

name: Sol Invictus
desc: Sol Invictus, the "Invincible" or "Unconquered Sun", was the official sun god of the late Roman Empire. The emperor Aurelian revived his cult in 274 CE, promoted him as the chief god of the empire and dedicated a new temple to him on 25 December 274; according to some scholars he also instituted on that day, the winter solstice of the Roman calendar, the festival Dies Natalis Solis Invicti. Scholars are divided on whether Sol Invictus was a Syrian sun god distinct from the old Latin god Sol or belonged to a single, continuous Roman cult of Sol. He often appeared on imperial coinage, and on that of Constantine I until 325/326. The last known inscription referring to him dates to 387 CE.

name: Saint Lucy's Day
desc: Saint Lucy's Day, also called the Feast of Saint Lucy, is a Christian feast day observed on 13 December in commemoration of Lucia of Syracuse, an early-fourth-century virgin martyr under the Diocletianic Persecution. According to legend she brought food to persecuted Christians hiding in the Roman catacombs, wearing a candle-lit wreath on her head to light her way. The feast became a universal feast of the Church in the 6th century. Because its date at one time coincided with the shortest day of the year, it is now widely celebrated as a festival of light, most widely in Scandinavia, Italy and Saint Lucia. The first modern-day Scandinavian celebration was held in 1928 in Stockholm.

name: Hogmanay
desc: Hogmanay is the Scots word for the last day of the old year and for the celebration of the New Year in the Scottish manner. The etymology of the word is obscure, the main modern theories deriving it from a French, Norse or Gaelic root; it is first recorded in a Latin entry of 1443 in the West Riding of Yorkshire and in Scots in 1604, in the records of Elgin. Its roots are speculated to reach back to the Norse celebration of the winter solstice and the Gaelic Samhain. The most widespread custom is first-footing, in which the first person to cross a friend's or neighbour's threshold after midnight brings symbolic gifts such as coal, shortbread, whisky and black bun.

name: Twelfth Night
desc: Twelfth Night, also known as Epiphany Eve, is a Christian festival on the last night of the Twelve Days of Christmas, marking the end of Christmastide and the coming of the Epiphany. Traditions place it on either 5 January or 6 January, depending on whether the counting begins on Christmas Day or on 26 December. In 567 the Council of Tours proclaimed the twelve days from Christmas to Epiphany a sacred and festive season. A popular custom was to hide a bean and a pea in a Twelfth-night cake, the man and the lady who found them becoming King and Queen for the night. Customs today include eating king cake, singing Christmas carols and chalking the door.
